title: "But Allah"
hook: then a yes: only Allah is worshiped

segments.voice: Yesterday, no god, la ilaha, and your line: first, no. When the thing you named tugged at you, did you manage one small no? Day one thousand sixty-five.

What do you do with a cleared room? Empty a closet or a garage, and there comes a moment: the junk is gone, the floor is bare, and there is a strange quiet. Leave it empty long enough and it fills back up with whatever wanders in. The shahadah doesn't leave the room empty. Right after the no comes one short word, illa, but, except. And after it, the one name it was clearing the room for.

La ilaha illallah. No god but Allah. Yesterday was the first half. Today, the hinge and the yes. First, the hinge: illa. It means but, or except. The sentence is built as a no to everything, then one exception. So it doesn't just say Allah is a god. It says nothing else is to be worshiped, only Allah. The no and the yes together make one claim. Second, who the yes is for. The Qur'an's own description is in the verse Muslims know as the Throne Verse, which opens, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal." The Alive, where yesterday's stars set and went dark. The Eternal, where everything that rises comes down again. The yes goes to the one thing that doesn't set. Third, what the yes does inside a person. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" The cleared room is not left cold. Something lives there now, and the verse calls the result rest. Fourth, how it's said. La ilaha illallah is short, and its sounds roll into one another, so it can be said under the breath while walking, cooking, or lying awake. A hadith in Tirmidhi's collection calls it the best remembrance, and some Sufi circles repeat it together, sometimes with the rhythm of the breath. Whether in a crowd or alone in a car, the shape is the same: first no, then yes.

The practice: illallah with the breath. Settle, and let your breathing find its own pace. If you pray, you can say la ilaha quietly as you breathe out, letting go, and illallah as you breathe in, letting the yes fill the space. If you'd rather not say the words, you can still feel the shape: out, clear the room; in, let something good fill it. No hurry, no counting. Just the two halves, over and over, as slowly as the breath wants to go. The bell holds the time.
But Allah. Illallah: the yes after the no, the one exception the whole sentence was built to hold. Today's word.
Your line: then, yes. Today, after you turn something down, notice what you turn toward in the space it leaves. Tomorrow, the second sentence: Muhammad is His messenger. Day one thousand sixty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims repeat la ilaha illallah as dhikr, remembrance, after prayers, on prayer beads, or quietly through the day; some Sufi circles say it together, sometimes in time with the breath.

myth: la ilaha illallah only says that Allah is a god
it's a no to everything and one exception: none is to be worshiped but Allah.
the Throne Verse calls Allah the Alive, the Eternal
"Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal."
la ilaha illallah can only be said in the formal prayer
it's said as remembrance anywhere: walking, cooking, lying awake.

fork.setup: you've cleared a room of everything that didn't belong. the shahadah has said its no. what comes next?
options: let a few old things back in.
fork.reveal: illallah: the sentence never leaves the room empty. the no exists to make space for the yes.

original.note: but Allah: the second half of la ilaha illallah, where illa means except.

trapdoor: what you thought: "but Allah" adds one more god to a list.
what it means: after a no to all of them, only Allah is to be worshiped.
what a scholar hears: a negation followed by an exception, which in Arabic restricts worship to Allah alone.

sources.quoted: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal.

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3383 (on la ilaha illallah as remembrance)

notes: Editor: hook no longer tells the listener what they know or feel; 'nothing else is worshiped' corrected to 'is to be worshiped' (teach, myth, trapdoor) as a claim about worthiness, not fact; Tirmidhi paraphrase now matches the hadith ('the best remembrance').
Pickthall 2:255 and 13:28 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording and punctuation.
Tirmidhi 3383 paraphrased as praising la ilaha illallah as a remembrance 'of the highest rank' (the hadith calls it the best dhikr); confirm the number and the paraphrase.

Breath pairing in the practice (out: la ilaha, in: illallah) is offered as one way, not as a prescribed method; some Sufi orders teach particular breath patterns. Keeper may prefer a different pairing or none.
Grammar note in the trapdoor (negation plus exception restricting worship) is a standard explanation; confirm.
